title: Abstraction, pointers and const
description: Abstract classes and pure virtual functions, pointers and references, and what const means in each position.

content.title: Abstraction with abstract classes
content.body:
Abstraction means showing what an object does and hiding how it does it. In C++, an abstract class describes that "what".

- A pure `virtual` function is declared with `= 0`: `virtual double area() const = 0;`
- A class with at least one pure `virtual` function is abstract: you cannot create an object of that type, by value, as an array element or with `new`.
- A derived class becomes concrete only when it overrides every pure `virtual` function with exactly the same signature, `const` included. Write `override` so that the compiler checks it.
- You use an abstract class through pointers or references: `Shape*` or `Shape&`.
- When objects are deleted through a base pointer, the base class needs a `virtual` destructor.
- A pure `virtual` function can still have a definition, written outside the class, that derived classes may call explicitly.

choices.text: It does not compile: Square is still abstract, because `area()` without `const` does not override `area() const`
It compiles, but calling `s.area()` is undefined behaviour
It does not compile: a pure `virtual` function needs a body

content.explanation: `const` is part of a member function's signature. `Square::area()` is a new function that hides `Shape::area()` instead of overriding it, so Square still has a pure `virtual` function and stays abstract. Declaring `double area() override` would have made the compiler report the mistake right on that line.

content.question:
Shape is an abstract class, and Circle is a concrete class derived from it (it overrides every pure `virtual` function).

```
Shape* p = new Circle(1.0);
```

Which of these lines compile?
content.explanation: Any line that creates a `Shape` object fails: `Shape s;`, `new Shape[2]` (an array of `Shape` objects) and `Shape copy = *p;` (a copy that would slice the Circle down to an abstract Shape). References and pointers to Shape are fine, including smart pointers that point to a Circle.

choices.text: Undefined behaviour, because `~Base()` is not `virtual` (in practice it often prints only B)
It does not compile: a `Derived*` cannot be stored in a `Base*`

content.explanation: Deleting a derived object through a base pointer whose destructor is not `virtual` is undefined behaviour. In practice only `~Base()` usually runs, so the Derived part is never cleaned up. With `virtual ~Base()`, it prints DB: the derived destructor runs first, then the base one.

While the Base constructor runs, the Derived part does not exist yet, so the object behaves as a Base and the `virtual` call resolves to `Base::hello()`. Once d is fully built, `d.hello()` calls `Derived::hello()`. Calling `virtual` functions from constructors and destructors rarely does what people expect.

choices.text: It does not compile: a pure `virtual` function cannot have a body
It does not compile: File is abstract

content.explanation: A pure `virtual` function may have a definition outside the class. Logger stays abstract, but derived classes can call that definition explicitly with `Logger::log()`. File overrides `log()`, so it is concrete.

content.title: Pointers and references
content.body:
A pointer stores an address. `&x` takes the address of x and `*p` gives access to the object p points to. `p->member` is short for `(*p).member`.

- A pointer can be null (`nullptr`), can be changed to point somewhere else, and can point to another pointer (`int** pp`).
- A local pointer that is not initialized contains garbage: dereferencing it, or dereferencing `nullptr`, is undefined behaviour.
- A reference is another name for an existing object. It must be initialized, it cannot be null, and it can never be made to refer to another object: `r = y;` assigns y's value to the object r refers to.
- Parameters are passed by value: a function that receives an `int*` gets a copy of the pointer. It can change the object pointed to, but not the caller's pointer, unless it receives `int*&` or `int**`.
- Never return a pointer or reference to a local variable: the variable is destroyed when the function returns.

content.explanation: q copies the address in p, so q points to a. Then p is changed to point to b, which does not affect q. `*q = 10` sets a to 10, and `*p += *q` adds 10 to b, which becomes 12.

choices.text: It does not compile: a reference cannot be assigned

content.explanation: A reference can never be changed to refer to another object. `r = b;` copies the value of b (2) into a. `r = 5;` then sets a to 5. b is never modified.

reset receives a copy of the pointer a: setting the copy to `nullptr` leaves a unchanged. resetRef receives a reference to the pointer b itself, so b becomes `nullptr`. A `bool` printed with `<<` shows 0 or 1.

content.question: Which snippets have undefined behaviour?

choices.text: `int* p = new int(1); delete p; delete p;`

content.explanation: Writing through an uninitialized pointer, dereferencing a pointer to a local variable that has been destroyed, and deleting the same memory twice are all undefined behaviour. Checking for `nullptr` before dereferencing is correct, and `**pp = 7` simply sets x to 7 through two levels of pointers.

content.title: const in every position
content.body:
Read a declaration from right to left: `const` applies to what is on its left, or to what is on its right when nothing is on its left.

- `const int* p` (same as `int const* p`): pointer to a `const int`. `*p` cannot be changed, p can.
- `int* const p`: `const` pointer to an `int`. p cannot be changed, `*p` can.
- `const int* const p`: neither can change.
- `const int& r`: cannot modify its target, and can also bind to a temporary such as `n + 1`. A non-`const int&` cannot.
- `void get() const`: a `const` member function cannot modify the object's members, except those declared `mutable`. Only `const` member functions can be called on a `const` object or through a `const` reference.
- Member functions can be overloaded on `const`: the `const` version is chosen for `const` objects.
- An `int*` converts implicitly to `const int*`, never the opposite. `const_cast` removes `const`, but modifying an object that was really defined `const` is undefined behaviour.

content.explanation: a points to a `const int`: the pointer can move, but `*a` cannot be modified. b is a `const` pointer: `*b` can be modified, but b cannot point elsewhere. c is both, so neither `*c` nor c can change. Note that x itself is not `const`; only the access through a and c is read-only.

content.question: Which declarations give `p` the same type as `const int* p = nullptr;`?

choices.text: `using IntPtr = int*; const IntPtr p = nullptr;`

content.explanation: `const int` and `int const` are the same type, and spaces around * change nothing. With an alias, `const` applies to the whole aliased type: `const IntPtr` is a `const` pointer to `int` (`int* const`), not a pointer to a `const int`.

choices.text: It compiles: `get()` does not modify value
It does not compile: `get()` is not a `const` member function, so it cannot be called through a `const` reference
It does not compile: a `const` reference cannot be passed to a function
It compiles, but calling `c.increment()` in show would also compile

content.explanation: The compiler does not look at what `get()` actually does: only member functions declared `const` can be called on a `const` object. The fix is `int get() const { return value; }`. `increment()` could never be `const`, since it modifies value.

choices.text: `reset()` does not compile, because value cannot be modified in a `const` member function
Both compile: `const` only applies to the return type
`read()` does not compile: a `const` member function cannot modify any member

content.explanation: In a `const` member function, this points to a `const` object, so members are read-only, except those declared `mutable`. `mutable` is meant for members that do not change the observable state, such as caches, counters or mutexes.

`n + 1` and 5 are temporaries (rvalues). A non-`const` reference cannot bind to a temporary, because modifications would be lost. A `const` reference can: the temporary lives until the end of the call.

choices.text: X is undefined behaviour, Y is fine

content.explanation: `const_cast` only removes `const` from the pointer type. Modifying an object that was defined `const` (a) is undefined behaviour: the compiler may have put it in read-only memory or replaced its uses by 1. b was never `const`, so modifying it through pb is defined.

choices.text: It does not compile: `show()` is defined twice

content.explanation: Member functions can be overloaded on `const`. b is not `const`, so the non-`const` version is chosen. cb is `const`, and r is a `const` reference (even though b itself is not `const`), so both call the `const` version.

content.instructions: Match each declaration with its meaning.

pairs.definition: Pointer to a `const int`: `*p` cannot change, p can
Const pointer to an `int`: p cannot change, `*p` can
Read-only reference that can also bind to a temporary
Pointer to a pointer to an `int`
Member function that cannot modify the object, except `mutable` members
Member that can change even in a `const` member function
Pure `virtual` function that makes the class abstract
